## Monday gave us a diagnosis

Cognition, conation, affect. Person and situation. The specificity principle.

Today those become **frameworks** — the tools that turn a diagnosis into a
strategy someone could fund and evaluate.

::: notes
Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4. Remind students that the specificity
principle from Box 8.5 is the reason TACT exists; they are the same idea at two
levels of abstraction.

**Pacing.** Full deck is 53 minutes; the core path is 45. Slides marked "If time is short, skip this slide" are the drop list: motivation/satisfaction and self-determination theory. Protect TACT, the reasoned action approach, and the pair rehearsal --- they map directly onto Friday items 1 and 3.
:::

## Today's question

What has to be true before a person performs a specific conservation behavior?

::: notes
Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.3. Write it on the board. Every
framework today is an answer to this question from a different angle.
:::

## What you should be able to do

By the end of today, you should be able to:

- define a target behavior using **TACT**;
- apply the **reasoned action approach** — attitudes, perceived norms,
  perceived behavioral control;
- explain **collective action** and why a perceived norm changes what an
  individual does; and
- use **affect**, **motivation**, and **satisfaction** to explain a behavior
  the other frameworks miss.

::: notes
Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 8, §§8.4.2–8.4.5. These four map onto Friday's
four response items in order.
:::

## Define the behavior first {background-color="#2f6b57" .section-slide}

You cannot manage, measure, or evaluate a behavior you have not specified.

::: notes
Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.3.
:::

## TACT

| Letter | Question | Weak | Strong |
|---|---|---|---|
| **T**arget | What or whom? | "the environment" | live wells, bilge, and drain plug |
| **A**ction | Do what, exactly? | "be responsible" | drain them |
| **C**ontext | Where, under what conditions? | "in general" | before leaving the north ramp |
| **T**ime | When, how often, for how long? | "someday" | every trip, 2027 open-water season |

::: {.key-idea}
"Boaters should care more about invasive species" fails all four. It cannot be
observed, so it cannot be managed.
:::

::: notes
Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.3 and Box 8.5. Do this live: take a
vague goal from the class and force all four columns. Then ask who would
observe it and where — if nobody can answer that, the behavior is still not
specified. Friday's item 1 is exactly this exercise.
:::

## The reasoned action approach

Behavioral **intention** is the most immediate predictor of behavior. Three
things shape it:

- **Attitudes** — the person's own evaluation of the behavior.
- **Perceived norms** — the social pressure to perform or avoid it.
- **Perceived behavioral control** (self-efficacy) — belief in one's ability to
  carry it out successfully.

::: notes
Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.3. Stress that these are three
separate levers. A favorable attitude with no self-efficacy produces nothing; so
does high self-efficacy against a hostile norm. This is why "raise awareness"
campaigns fail when awareness was never the binding constraint.
:::

## Which lever is actually broken?

::: {.fragment}
**Attitude is fine, norm is fine, control is low** → make the behavior easier,
teach the skill, remove the time cost.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Attitude is fine, control is fine, norm is low** → make others' behavior
visible; recruit the groups people belong to.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Attitude is the problem** → this is the rarest case in conservation, and the
one most campaigns assume.
:::

::: notes
Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.3. Reveal one at a time. This slide is
the practical payoff of the whole week: the diagnosis determines the
intervention, and getting it wrong wastes the budget. Friday's case brief is
built so that the third box is demonstrably not the problem.
:::

## Collective action {background-color="#123f5a" .section-slide}

Some behaviors only make sense if others are doing them too.

::: notes
Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.2.
:::

## Individual factors and collective factors

The collective interest model holds that behavior is influenced by **individual
factors** and **collective factors** together.

In the Montana bear-attractant work (Box 8.4):

- Different attractant-securing behaviors were associated with **different**
  suites of individual factors.
- **Collective factors were influential across the board.**
- Landowners who believed their neighbors were securing attractants, and
  expected them to keep doing so, were **30% to 100% more likely** to secure
  their own.

::: notes
Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, Box 8.4. The most consistent individual
predictor was biocentric belief, but the collective effect was the one that
held across every behavior. Practitioners responded by changing the messaging
to convey normative information, reduce feelings of isolation, and invest in
professionals who start conversations among landowners.
:::

## Why this changes the intervention

::: {.key-idea}
If a person's behavior depends on what they believe others are doing, then a
message about the harm of the problem is aimed at the wrong variable.
:::

A perceived norm can be wrong. People routinely underestimate how many others
are complying — and act on the underestimate.

::: notes
Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.2. This distinction matters on Friday:
a survey item asking "do most others drain their boats?" measures a *perceived*
norm, not a compliance rate. Groups that treat it as a measured rate have made
an error the brief warns about.
:::

## Affect: emotions are not decoration

Emotions influence perception, judgment, memory, and behavior. They are
psychological **and** physiological responses to events, situations, or stimuli.

- Seeing a robin at a feeder, or a raccoon at a trash can, can evoke anything
  from appreciation and awe to fear or disgust.
- In a deer-management study, emotions influenced the **acceptability of
  management options**.

::: notes
Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.4. Affect is a relative newcomer in
this field, which is why it is often missing from agency analysis. Note the
management consequence: emotion shapes not only behavior but whether a proposed
action is seen as acceptable at all. Resentment toward an agency is affect, and
it is actionable evidence.
:::

## Motivation and satisfaction

**Motivation** is why people act. **Satisfaction** is what they get out of it.

Decker and Connelly's three orientations:

- **Affiliative** — social interaction and bonding.
- **Achievement** — reaching a performance goal.
- **Appreciative** — peace, belonging, stress reduction.

::: notes
Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.5. The management consequence is that
agencies must manage more than bag limits: they manage experiential outcomes.
Two people performing the identical behavior may be seeking entirely different
things, and a program that serves one may not serve the other.

**If time is short, skip this slide.** The thread survives without it.
:::

## Self-determination theory

Motivation is driven by three basic psychological needs:

- **Autonomy** — feeling in control of one's own actions.
- **Competence** — feeling effective in an environment.
- **Relatedness** — connection with others.

::: {.key-idea}
A program that tells people what to do, implies they are doing it wrong, and
isolates them, undercuts all three at once.
:::

::: notes
Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §8.4.5. When conservation programs meet
these needs, participants show higher intrinsic motivation. Connect to Friday:
an enforcement-only framing can damage autonomy and relatedness even when the
rule itself is correct.

**If time is short, skip this slide.** The thread survives without it.
:::

## Pair rehearsal: match the lever

With a partner, name the framework and the lever you would pull:

> "There's a line of eight boats and a guy in a hurry behind me. I'm not
> holding that up for ten minutes."

> "On the tournament circuit everybody decons. You'd get talked about if you
> didn't."

> "Every sign out here is written like we did something wrong."

::: notes
Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §§8.4.2–8.4.4. Answers: perceived
behavioral control plus a situational constraint; perceived norm, strongly
positive; affect, with a self-determination reading available. All three
quotations are in Friday's case brief, so this is direct rehearsal for items
2 and 3.
:::

## Friday

Read the **Week 07 Case Brief: The Thornapple Lake Decontamination Problem**
before class. Everything you need is in it.

A $180,000 campaign changed nothing — because **92% of boaters already agreed**
invasive mussels are harmful, before and after.

::: notes
Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 8, §§8.4–8.4.5. Tell students the roles this
week are target behavior lead, person factors lead, and situation and norms
lead, and that the roster is published. Warn them that the $220,000 budget
arithmetic is part of the grade.
:::

## Close

::: {.key-idea}
A strategy that cannot name its target behavior, the lever it is pulling, and
the indicator that would show it working is not a strategy. It is a hope.
:::

::: notes
Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 8, §8.5. Preview Week 8: the same decline
problem viewed from sociology, where the unit of analysis stops being the
individual.
:::
